prompt.context: Two of your business school classmates decided to open a video rental store near the Wharton campus despite recent industry trends. Their first two and a half years were wildly successful — they bought matching Porsches and a townhouse in Society Hill. However, over the past 12 months profits have dramatically fallen after that period of strong profit and revenue growth. They have called you (now at a prominent strategy consulting firm in Philadelphia) for help, saying they do not know what happened and that their mortgage and car payments are getting harder to meet.
prompt.question: What do you think the problem is? Help your former classmates diagnose why profits have dramatically fallen at their video rental store.

clarifying_info.a: Costs have not materially changed. Video rental is a high fixed-cost business (rent, videos, and labor are all largely fixed).
No, management has not changed the price charged per rental.

clarifying_info.q: Are fewer customers coming to the store, or are existing customers renting fewer videos?
clarifying_info.a: Store traffic (number of customers coming in) has fallen.

clarifying_info.q: Has a new video rental store opened in the area?
Has a new movie theatre opened in the area?
Have there been economic changes in the area?

framework: Start with the profit equation: Profit = Revenue - Costs. Determine whether costs have risen or revenues have fallen (or both).
Establish that this is a high fixed-cost business (rent, video inventory, labor), making profitability highly sensitive to revenue/volume changes rather than cost creep.
Break Revenue into its drivers: Number of customers × Average rentals per customer × Price per rental. Since price is unchanged, focus on volume.

Distinguish between two volume problems: (a) Traffic problem — fewer customers entering the store (external/market issue), or (b) Share-of-wallet problem — same customers renting fewer videos per visit (internal/execution issue).
If traffic is down, generate hypotheses about causes: new competitive entrants (other video stores, movie theatres) vs. macro/economic factors vs. structural market shift.
Broaden the competitive frame: define the client's business as 'home movie entertainment,' not just 'video rental.' This expands the competitive set to any service delivering movies at home.

Identify the likely root cause: a new substitute technology or service (cable, pay-per-view, video-on-demand, delivery services) has grown rapidly, reducing the addressable market for store-based video rentals.

questions.prompt: If profits have declined, what are the two primary causes you would investigate first?
questions.guidance: Revenues have declined OR costs have increased. Candidate should state this profit equation decomposition explicitly before diving into specifics.

questions.prompt: Why is cost probably not the root problem here?
questions.guidance: Video rental is a high fixed-cost business — rent, video inventory, and labor do not flex much with rental volume. Therefore profit swings are primarily driven by revenue/utilization changes, not cost changes.

questions.prompt: Revenue = price × volume. Price is unchanged. How would you further decompose the volume decline?
questions.guidance: Volume = number of customers (traffic) × average rentals per customer visit. Candidate should articulate both levers and propose how to measure each (e.g., door counter for traffic; register receipts for rentals per visit).

math.setup: Revenue = Customers × Avg Rentals per Customer × Price per Rental. Price is held constant, so Revenue change = f(Customers, Avg Rentals).
steps: Compare door-counter data year-over-year to isolate traffic change.
Compare register receipts year-over-year to isolate rentals-per-customer change.
Determine which metric has deteriorated more.
math.answer: Data shows traffic (number of customers entering the store) has fallen — this is a traffic problem, not a share-of-wallet problem.

questions.prompt: Traffic is down. What are the hypotheses for why fewer customers are coming to the store?
questions.guidance: Strong answer distinguishes macro factors (economic downturn, demographic shift) from competitive factors (new video store, new movie theatre, substitute entertainment). Candidate should note that video rental demand is relatively inelastic to economic conditions and therefore lean toward competitive/structural explanations.

questions.prompt: No new video stores or movie theatres have opened. What might still explain the traffic decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate should broaden the definition of the client's business. The client is not just in 'video rental' — they are in 'home movie entertainment.' The competitive set therefore includes any service that delivers movies to homes: cable TV expansion, pay-per-view (PPV), video-on-demand (VOD), DVD delivery services, or early streaming. A new or rapidly growing substitute in this broader category would reduce the market for store-based rentals.

brainstorming.prompt: What other competitive or market factors might explain a sustained decline in traffic to a video rental store near a university campus?

categories.name: Substitute technologies / services
ideas: Cable TV adding more movie channels

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: National chain (e.g., Blockbuster) opening a nearby location
Online rental platforms gaining adoption among students

categories.name: Demand-side / customer behavior
ideas: Student population preferences shifting toward other entertainment (gaming, concerts, bars)
Customers buying DVDs instead of renting

categories.name: Internal / operational
ideas: Selection no longer meeting customer preferences (older titles, limited new releases)
Poor customer service driving customers away
Inconvenient hours or location changes nearby

recommendation: The most likely root cause is structural market disruption: a substitute home-entertainment technology or service (cable, PPV, VOD, or delivery) has grown rapidly in the area, shrinking the addressable market for store-based video rentals.
The business model faces a secular headwind; a purely operational fix will not restore prior profit levels if the market itself has contracted.
risks: If the market contraction continues, even significant operational improvements may not return the store to prior profitability.
Investing in inventory or marketing without addressing the root competitive shift could accelerate losses.
next_steps: Quantify the traffic decline year-over-year and benchmark against regional video rental industry data to confirm whether this is store-specific or industry-wide.
Survey customers to understand which alternative entertainment options they have adopted and why.
Evaluate strategic options: differentiate on selection/service, partner with complementary services, or consider exit/pivot if market decline is confirmed as structural.
